To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
γ-secretase inhibition decreases amyloid-β peptide levels in plasma and cerebrospinal fluids comparably in young plaque-free and aged plaque-bearing Tg2576 transgenic mice.
the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT reduces Aβ levels in plasma and CSF comparably in young and aged Tg2576 transgenic mice.
γ-secretase inhibitors, when administered to young (plaque free) or old (plaque bearing) Tg25776 mice, dose-dependently reduce Aβ levels in plasma and cerebrospinal fluids (CSF) but not in brains.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role that amyloid-β peptide (Aβ) plays in Alzheimer's disease (AD), a neurodegenerative disease that is the leading cause of dementia in the United States.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
the development of new drugs to treat Alzheimer's disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
γ-secretase inhibitors reduce Aβ levels in plasma and CSF, and that this response is not dependent on the presence of amyloid plaques.

CSF and/or plasma levels of Aβ can be used as a biomarker for γ-secretase inhibitors.
